lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Percent Repair: Unknown Whole and Decimal Division
lessons.previous_learning: Day 14 showed specific scale errors: 72 as 30% of a whole, 48 as 20% of a whole, 84/0.35, 45/0.30, plus incomplete discount work.
lessons.course_context: Repair exact missed structures before any new percent work.
learning_objectives: Explain why dividing by a decimal below 1 makes the quotient larger.
Finish both outputs in multi-step questions.
lessons.why_it_matters: Reliable math means repairing exact errors before carrying them forward.

vocabulary.definition: the complete quantity when part and percent are known
putting the answer back into the original relationship

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: you are starting with yesterday’s missed structures because your concept is stronger than your execution. Whole = Part / decimal percent. When percent <100%, the whole must be larger than the part. Scale decimal division by multiplying dividend and divisor by the same power of ten.

worked_examples.title: Decimal division
worked_examples.explanation: Because .30<1, answer must exceed 42; scale to 4200/30.

worked_examples.title: Discount
worked_examples.explanation: Find discount, then subtract; both are required.

guided_practice.prompt: Repair round: 72 is 30% of what whole; 48 is 20% of what whole; 84/0.35; 45/0.30; $180 discounted 15% with both outputs.

independent_practice.prompt: 54 is 30% of what whole? Reverse check.
36 is 24% of what whole? Estimate first.
42 students are 28% of a program. Find the whole.
Repair the claim 64/0.40=25.6 and explain why impossible.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. Begin by explaining why he is repairing these exact problems: yesterday showed scale/place-value errors, not lack of intelligence. This is not punishment. Use whiteboard_draw on a DIFFERENT analogous example: PART/PERCENT/WHOLE boxes, scaling decimal division by 100, and a reverse-check loop. Never draw or say an assigned final answer. Do not move to transfer practice until the five repair items are correct and complete.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Day 14 showed être/avoir choice is secure but de/d' after pas is not automatic.
lessons.course_context: Repair one pattern only before new grammar.
lessons.why_it_matters: Automatic grammar frees attention for communication.
lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: you already choose être and avoir well. Today fix only this: after pas, un/une/des becomes de, or d' before a vowel sound. Say each sentence aloud first.

worked_examples.title: Vowel
worked_examples.explanation: Use d' before a vowel sound.

exit_ticket.prompt: Mastery: at least 9/10 correct without a model.
exit_ticket.answer: At least nine correct de/d' transformations.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. Oral first. On the whiteboard, show only the pattern ne/n' + AVOIR + pas + de/d' + noun and one different example. If he uses un/une/des after pas, say only: Check the noun phrase after pas. Require the full corrected sentence.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.lesson_title: Convex Lens Ray Models: Camera and Eye
lessons.previous_learning: Day 14 showed Atticus knows lenses redirect light but called lens surfaces flat and did not yet secure the ray/focal model.
lessons.course_context: Repair curvature and ray model, then apply to camera and eye.
learning_objectives: Draw parallel rays toward a focal region.
Explain camera sensor and eye retina applications.
lessons.why_it_matters: The same refraction model explains important optical technologies.

vocabulary.definition: where parallel rays meet in a simple model

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: a convex lens is curved, not flat. Rays hitting different parts of its curved boundary arrive at different angles and refract differently. Cameras direct rays toward sensors; eyes direct rays toward the retina.

worked_examples.title: Parallel rays
worked_examples.problem: Three parallel rays enter a convex lens.
worked_examples.solution: Outer rays bend toward the axis and focal region.
worked_examples.explanation: Curved boundaries create different angles and refraction.

worked_examples.title: Camera
worked_examples.problem: How does a camera lens form an image?
worked_examples.solution: It directs scene rays toward the sensor.
worked_examples.explanation: Controlled refraction organizes the light pattern.

worked_examples.title: Eye
worked_examples.problem: What does the eye lens do?
worked_examples.solution: It helps focus light toward the retina.
worked_examples.explanation: The retina detects the light pattern.

guided_practice.prompt: Explain edge vs center rays, then draw lens, principal axis, three parallel rays, and focal point.

independent_practice.prompt: Connect camera lens behavior to the bent-pencil refraction idea.
Correct: The eye lens makes the object bigger.

exit_ticket.prompt: Why does curvature matter in a convex lens?
exit_ticket.answer: Curvature changes boundary angles so rays refract differently.

exit_ticket.prompt: How does a camera or eye use refraction?
exit_ticket.answer: It redirects incoming rays toward a sensor or retina to form an organized image.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach first and speak directly to Atticus. Proactively use whiteboard_draw: clear board, draw principal axis, convex lens, three parallel rays, then add refracted rays one by one and mark focal point. After teaching, ask him to explain the rays. For assigned diagrams, use a different example or blank scaffold, never the completed assigned answer. Draw a second comparison: CAMERA SENSOR vs EYE RETINA.
